title: Analysis of cereulide incident reveals persistent challenges in infant formula
summary:
Three key issues have been identified by European countries asked for feedback about the response to infant formula contaminated with cereulide.

Cereulide was found in arachidonic acid (ARA) oil, a raw material from Cabio Biotech, a Chinese supplier. Cereulide is a toxin produced by certain strains of Bacillus cereus.

**_By Cynthia Joseph_**

Most consumers assume that everything listed on a food label has passed through careful government scrutiny before landing on store shelves. That assumption hasn't always held true. For years, a regulatory mechanism known as "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS) has let food companies skip the FDA's formal review process for new additives — and in many instances, add them to products without ever informing federal regulators.

**How the loophole works**  
Congress created the GRAS category back in 1958 to spare well-established, everyday substances — things like table salt, vinegar, and baking soda — from the expensive, drawn-out testing required of genuinely new chemical additives. That made sense at the time. But the system had a flaw: companies were allowed to assemble their own panels of hired scientists, have those panels sign off on a new ingredient's safety, and start using it commercially—all without ever alerting the FDA or the public.

According to consumer advocacy organizations, this quiet pathway let thousands of substances slip into the American food supply largely unnoticed, leaving physicians, researchers, and toxicologists with an incomplete picture of what people were actually consuming.

**The case for mandatory disclosure**  
A proposed FDA rule would require companies to formally notify the agency before using a GRAS ingredient, replacing today's opt-in honor system. This shift would matter in a few key respects.

title: Pork products linked to rise in Swiss hepatitis E cases
summary:
Title: Pork products linked to rise in Swiss hepatitis E cases

URL Source: https://www.foodsafetynews.com/2026/11/pork-products-linked-to-rise-in-swiss-hepatitis-e-cases/

Published Time: 2026-11-12T05:01:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Plus: A summary of 2025 recalls in Switzerland

![Image 1: Pork products linked to rise in Swiss hepatitis E cases](https://storage.ghost.io/c/43/4e/434e508a-5e2f-4102-a53d-00bca10bb4bf/content/images/size/w30/2026/11/dreamstime_hepatitis-e.png)

Published:November 12, 2026, 12:01 am

Last updated:November 12, 2026, 12:00 am

Researchers have been unable to identify the specific food item that caused a spike in hepatitis E infections in Switzerland, but some pork products were indicated.

Scientists studied the unprecedented increase in hepatitis E virus (HEV) cases from January to May 2021. Findings were published in the [journal IJID One Health](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949915126000557?ref=foodsafetynews.com).

Overall, 55 cases reported at least one symptom of infection, while 30 reported no symptoms and 29 people had to be hospitalized because of their HEV infection. Two men over the age of 65 died. For one the cause of death was neurological complications after HEV infection.

Americans went to the polls this month with food issues top of mind. Rather than improve the food system, the last Congress and President Trump made matters worse by further fueling inflation, slashing federal feeding programs, and undermining food safety.

Rising grocery store prices were a top issue for voters in the last election,[driven by](https://www.cspi.org/cspi-news/why-are-groceries-so-expensive-what-you-need-know?ref=foodsafetynews.com)tariffs, supply chain disruptions, and the fuel shortages from foreign wars. Food price inflation puts an immediate, highly tangible squeeze on household budgets.
